In the summer of 1858, London smelled so bad that Parliament ran away.
Members of Parliament fled their own building, holding handkerchiefs over their faces.
The cause? The River Thames, right outside their windows.
For years, London had poured its sewage straight into the river. And millions of Londoners drank that water.
That summer was one of the hottest ever recorded. And the river began to cook.
The stench got so strong that Parliament hung curtains soaked in chemicals, just to keep working.
Doctors believed that disease spread through bad smells. So a smell like this meant one thing: cholera.
They were wrong about the smell. But the panic worked.
Within eighteen days, Parliament passed a law to rebuild London's sewers.
The engineer Joseph Bazalgette built over a thousand miles of sewers, using more than three hundred million bricks.
The sewage now flowed far out of the city, and London's cholera outbreaks finally ended.
Millions of lives were saved, because a river stank.
And many of those sewers are still working today.
